titre: Did the Great Fire of London (1666) Really Kill Only Six People?
accroche: 13,200 houses gone up in smoke in four days, and a traditional toll of six deaths that several historians consider far too low.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the night of September 2, 1666, a fire breaks out in a bakery on Pudding Lane in London. Driven by an east wind and fed by wooden houses packed tightly together, it ravages the City for four days. The material toll is beyond doubt: between 13,200 and 13,500 houses destroyed, 86 or 87 parish churches and Old St. Paul's Cathedral reduced to ashes, tens of thousands of Londoners left homeless. One question remains that textbooks repeat without always weighing it: how many people died in the fire? The most-cited answer is astonishing given the damage: six.

## A Figure No Methodical Count Supports

This figure of six deaths (eight according to the historian Stephen Porter, “in single digits” according to Adrian Tinniswood) is backed by no on-the-ground census: the *London Gazette*, the official newspaper that followed the fire day by day, does not record a single death. The historian Jacob Field, who has looked closely at the question, concedes that the true total may have been “higher than the traditional figure of six,” while judging it unlikely to run into the hundreds. The disagreement among historians is therefore less about whether there was an undercount than about its scale.

## What the Traditional Figure Could Not See

Other historians, foremost among them Neil Hanson, go much further and put forward a toll in the hundreds, even thousands. Their argument has two parts. First, the City's poor, servants, and residents without recognized family were not counted with the same care as property owners or heads of household: some of the potential victims structurally escape any written trace. Second, according to Hanson, the heat given off by such a blaze far exceeded that of an ordinary house fire, to the point that it could have consumed some bodies entirely, or left only rare bone fragments, with no identifiable remains and not even a disappearance reported as linked to the fire.

The shift, then, lies not in the figure itself, which remains elusive, but in what it reveals: a disaster's death toll always tells as much about the attention a society paid to its dead as about the catastrophe it claims to describe. Six deaths for 13,000 houses is not good statistical news: it is the trace of what a 17th-century register was not trying to see.

repere.texte: The Great Fire of London destroyed between 13,200 and 13,500 houses and 86 or 87 parish churches in four days; the traditionally accepted toll is only six deaths, while the historian Neil Hanson estimates it in the hundreds, even thousands.
repere.source: Wikipedia, “Great Fire of London,” based on Jacob Field, Stephen Porter, Adrian Tinniswood, and Neil Hanson

carte.punch: 13,200 houses burned in 4 days: the traditional toll counts only six deaths.
carte.idee: The Great Fire of London (1666) destroys about 13,200 houses and 87 churches. The traditional toll of six deaths rests on no methodical count: the London Gazette does not record a single death. Neil Hanson judges the true toll to be much heavier, in the hundreds or even thousands.

quiz.question: Why do several historians consider the traditional toll of six deaths in the Great Fire of London unreliable?
choix: Because King Charles II had banned any publication about the fire
Because the London Gazette recorded no deaths and the poor were poorly counted
Because St. Paul's Cathedral held the city's only registers, destroyed along with it
Because the authorities deliberately understated the figure to avoid panic
quiz.explication: The official newspaper, the London Gazette, recorded no deaths, and the poor, servants, and people without recognized family largely escaped the counts of the time: nothing indicates a royal ban on publication, centralized registers at St. Paul's, or a deliberate understatement.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when did the Great Fire of London begin?
choix: On November 5, 1666, near St. Paul's Cathedral
On September 2, 1665, in a warehouse in the Port of London
On September 2, 1666, in a tavern on Fleet Street
On September 2, 1666, in a bakery on Pudding Lane
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The fire broke out on the night of September 2, 1666, in a bakery on Pudding Lane, before spreading through the City on an east wind.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What toll does Neil Hanson put forward, at the opposite extreme from the traditional figure of six deaths?
choix: Exactly eight deaths, as the historian Stephen Porter argues
Several hundred, even thousands of deaths
No additional deaths, the figure of six being reliable
A single-digit figure, as Adrian Tinniswood argues
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Neil Hanson estimates that the real toll could run into the hundreds, even thousands, far beyond the traditional figure of six deaths accepted by other historians.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Neil Hanson's argument, why might the heat of the fire have skewed the death count?
choix: It could have consumed some bodies entirely or left only rare bone fragments
It destroyed the parish registers that listed the inhabitants
It kept rescuers from reaching the affected neighborhoods for weeks
It caused an epidemic that killed residents after the fire
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Hanson argues that the heat, far greater than that of a house fire, could have consumed some bodies entirely or left only rare bone fragments, with no identifiable trace.
